summary: This document defines DNS functions for a Drone Remote Identification Protocol (DRIP) Identity Management Entity. Built around DRIP Entity Tags, it sets up a hierarchical registry for registering and looking up drone identities.

plainLanguage.summary: Every drone gets a name tag, and this sets up a phone book so authorities can find who a tag belongs to.

subtitle: How drone identity tags are looked up in the DNS, using the IPv6 reverse tree as a registry.

tldr.problem: Broadcast Remote ID can only carry a little information, so observers need a trustworthy place to look up the keys, certificates and pointers that go with a drone's DRIP Entity Tag (DET).
tldr.mechanism: A DET is an IPv6 address, so RFC 9886 maps it into the ip6.arpa reverse tree, delegates the DET prefix down a hierarchy of registries, and defines two new DNS record types: HHIT (type 67) and BRID (type 68).
tldr.outcome: Public DET data lives in authoritative DNS servers, with an IANA registry for the top of the hierarchy. DNSSEC is required for self-signed apex entities and recommended for the rest.

today: RFC 9886 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Drone IDs Need a Registry
sections.content:
Registries are fundamental to Unmanned Aircraft System (UAS) Remote Identification (RID). Only very limited information can be sent via Broadcast RID, but extended information is sometimes needed. The most essential element is the UAS ID, the unique key for looking up that extended information.

When a DRIP Entity Tag (DET) from RFC 9374 is used as the UAS ID, extended information can be retrieved from a DRIP Identity Management Entity (DIME). This document assumes the DIME is a function of a UAS Service Supplier (USS), though a DIME can be independent or handled by another entity.

Authoritative DNS name servers provide the public information: cryptographic keys, endorsements and certificates of DETs, and pointers to private information. The RFC does not specify the AAA mechanisms that private registries use to protect personally identifiable information.
sections.plainLanguage: A drone can only shout a tiny bit about itself while flying. So it shouts its name tag, and you look the name up in a phone book to learn more.

sections.title: DETs as IPv6 Addresses in the Reverse Tree
sections.content:
A DET is a 128-bit value that is an IPv6 address, intended primarily as an identifier rather than a locator. RFC 9374 assigns the prefix 2001:30::/28 for DETs, whose reverse-lookup domain is 3.0.0.1.0.0.2.ip6.arpa.. The IAB has administrative control of this domain name.

The 28-bit Hierarchy ID splits into a 14-bit Registered Assigning Authority (RAA) and a 14-bit HHIT Domain Authority (HDA). Because DNS reverse names work on four-bit nibbles, an RAA borrows the upper two bits of its HDA space. An RAA's prefix becomes 2001:3x:xxx0::/44 and an HDA's becomes 2001:3x:xxxy:yy00::/56. As a result, the HDA values 0, 4096, 8192 and 12288 are reserved for the RAA's own operational use.

The RFC preallocates RAAs based on ISO 3166-1 numeric country codes, to support international use of DETs. Policy for running a DIME at any level is out of scope, and for country-based RAAs the RFC expects national authorities, presumably the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA), to decide.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag is built like a street address: country, then town, then house. The phone book follows the same order, so you find the right page quickly.

sections.title: Registry Models and Delegation
sections.content:
DRIP roughly follows the DNS registrant-registrar-registry model. The registrant is the end user who owns or controls the aircraft, registrars manage the registrant's dealings with the registry, and the registry runs the zone apex with delegation information. There can only be one registry for a domain name.

The RFC says this model could add costs and complexity, and sketches alternatives. Blocks of addresses could be delegated from 3.0.0.1.0.0.2.ip6.arpa. to a third party chosen by the CAA, much as IP address space is handed to an ISP, and in principle a UAS manufacturer or vendor could play that role. Dynamic registration, where an operator registers records before a flight and deletes them afterwards, might work in controlled environments but may not scale because each device needs credentials to update the DNS infrastructure.

Pricing, renewals and agreements are left to the CAA, perhaps in consultation with local stakeholders.
sections.plainLanguage: There are a few ways to run the phone book: like a normal website name shop, like an internet provider handing out blocks, or by signing up only on flight days. The RFC leaves the choice to each country.

sections.title: Public Information and Lookups
sections.content:
All information classified as public is stored in authoritative name servers. DETs sit under ip6.arpa., nibble reversed as in RFC 3596, and a DET's name MUST resolve to an HHIT record. Other record types MAY be present, such as DS records when DNSSEC is used. For UAS RID, the BRID record MUST be present to provide the Broadcast Endorsements.

A lookup differs from an ordinary reverse lookup: clients query for HHIT and/or BRID records rather than PTR records. For example, the DET 2001:30::1 is looked up at the 32-nibble reversed name ending in 3.0.0.1.0.0.2.ip6.arpa..

DNSSEC MUST be used for apex entities (those with a self-signed Canonical Registration Certificate) and is RECOMMENDED for others. A DIME that uses it SHOULD define a framework for algorithms and key management.
sections.plainLanguage: You look up the tag the way you would look up a street address backwards, and the answer is the tag's key and certificate instead of a house name.

sections.title: The HHIT and BRID Records
sections.content:
The HHIT resource record (RRType 67) holds HHIT-specific metadata that the existing HIP record cannot carry. It does not replace the HIP record from RFC 8005. Its advantage is a mandatory Canonical Registration Certificate, a public key signed by the registrar or another trust anchor. The data MUST be CBOR, shown in zone files as base64. It has three required fields: a numeric hhit-entity-type, a hid-abbreviation string of up to 15 characters, and the certificate as X.509 DER. The certificate MAY be self-signed when the entity is an apex.

Absent local policy, the HID abbreviation MUST be the four-character hexadecimal RAA and HDA with a separator, so RAA 10 and HDA 20 become 000A 0014.

The BRID resource record (RRType 68) holds the static parts of Broadcast RID information. For DRIP its main job is to hold one or more Broadcast Endorsements from RFC 9575 in the auth field, generated by the registrar on registration. Field names come from the ASTM data dictionary, and application-specific fields are carried and authenticated but treated as opaque.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone book entry has two cards. One holds the tag's key and its stamp of approval. The other holds the short facts the drone already shouts, so you can compare them.

sections.title: IANA Registries and RAA Allocation
sections.content:
IANA manages the reverse domain for the DET prefix and liaises, as needed, with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) to verify delegations to CAAs. The RFC records two registries under the Drone Remote ID Protocol group: RAA Allocations and HHIT Entity Types.

RAA values are 14 bits. Values 4 to 3999 are ISO 3166-1 countries under IESG Approval, and each nation gets 4 RAAs, so a shorter 2001:3x:xx00::/40 prefix MAY be delegated to each CAA. Values 8192 to 15359 are unassigned and First Come First Served. Values 15360 to 16383 are Private Use: IANA will not delegate them, so reverse lookups there can only come from private DNS servers, for example for experimentation.

HHIT Entity Types are First Come First Served. Initial values include 1 for a DIME, 5 for an Apex, 9 for an RAA, 13 for an HDA, 16 for an Unmanned Aircraft and 20 for a Pilot.
sections.plainLanguage: A global office keeps the master list of which country owns which page in the phone book, and keeps some pages blank for practice.

sections.title: Security and Key Exposure
sections.content:
Registrars and registries SHOULD follow common DNS best practice, including DNSSEC, except where national regulations prevent it. If DNSSEC is used, a DNSSEC Practice Statement SHOULD be published, and a self-signed entity MUST use DNSSEC. Without it, DRIP entities are exposed to DNS spoofing and bogus data. The RFC lists denial of service, replay attacks, impersonation or cloning of UAVs, hijacking of DET registrations and injection of corrupt metadata as threats.

Without DNSSEC, clients MUST walk the tree of certificates, looking up the HHIT record at each level to verify inclusion in the hierarchy, because the ORCHID hash in a DET is short. That certificate chain is the only way without DNSSEC to prove valid registration. Endorsements in the BRID record, when present, MUST also be validated.

Because DETs are built on asymmetric keys, the public key must be revealed. When practical, it is RECOMMENDED not to publish any records under a DET's domain name until another party needs them.
sections.plainLanguage: If the phone book can be tricked, someone could copy a drone's name tag. Extra seals on the book, and checking each page's stamp up the chain, stop that.
